title: Objects and Classes

items.title: What is an Object?
items.content:
In Python, an object is an instance of a class. A class is a blueprint that defines attributes (data) and methods (behavior). For example, a class named Car can be used to create objects like my_car. Each object stores its own state. Here is a simple example:

```python
class Car:
    pass

my_car = Car()
print('my_car is an object of type', type(my_car))
```

Notice that my_car is created from the Car class, making it an object.
items.explanation: In Python, an object is an instance of a class. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes a class in Python?
options: A variable that stores a single value
A blueprint used to create objects
A function that performs a calculation
items.correct_answer: A blueprint used to create objects
items.explanation: A class acts as a template or blueprint. You define attributes and methods inside it, and then create objects from it.

items.title: Defining a Class and Creating an Object
items.content:
To define a class, use the class keyword followed by the class name. By convention, class names use PascalCase. After defining the class, you create an object by calling the class name as if it were a function. Here is a complete example:

```python
class Dog:
    pass

buddy = Dog()
print('buddy is an instance of', type(buddy).__name__)
```

The line `buddy = Dog()` creates an object named buddy. The `pass` statement is a placeholder when the class body is empty.
items.explanation: To define a class, use the class keyword followed by the class name. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: Match each term to its role in object-oriented programming.
options: Class: a specific instance; Object: a general template
Class: a general template; Object: a specific instance
Class: a method; Object: an attribute
Class: a function; Object: a variable
items.correct_answer: Class: a general template; Object: a specific instance
items.explanation: A class defines the structure and behavior, while an object is a concrete entity created from that class.

items.explanation: If you call the class to create an object but do not store it in a variable, the object is created and immediately discarded because there is no reference to it.

micro_lesson.title: Defining a Class with the class Keyword
micro_lesson.content:
In Python, a class is a blueprint for creating objects. You define a class using the `class` keyword, followed by the class name. By convention, class names use PascalCase. Inside the class, you define attributes and methods. Here is an example:

```python
class Dog:
    pass
```

The `pass` statement is a placeholder that does nothing but allows the syntax to be valid. Once defined, you can create an instance (object) of the class using the class name followed by parentheses.

items.prompt: Complete the code by filling in the blank: `class ___:`
items.explanation: The `class` keyword introduces a new class definition. `Dog` is the class name, written in PascalCase. The colon `:` must follow the class name to start the class block.

micro_lesson.title: Using __init__ and self
micro_lesson.content:
The `__init__` method is a special method called a constructor. It initializes an object's attributes when the object is created. The first parameter of any instance method is always `self`, which refers to the current instance of the class. Here is an example:

```python
class Car:
    def __init__(self, brand):
        self.brand = brand
```

When you create a `Car` object, Python automatically calls `__init__` to set up the `brand` attribute on that specific instance.

items.prompt: Fill in the blank to complete the constructor: `def ___ (self, color):`
items.explanation: `__init__` is the special constructor method in Python classes. It is automatically invoked when a new object is instantiated.

micro_lesson.title: Correct Order for Class Definition and Instantiation
micro_lesson.content:
To use a class, you must first define it, then create an instance of it. The class definition includes the class header and its methods. After the class is defined, you can call the class name with arguments to create an object. Here is the proper sequence:

```python
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title

my_book = Book('Python Basics')
print(my_book.title)
```

Notice that the class is defined before any object is created. The `my_book` variable holds the instance, and you access its attribute with dot notation.

items.prompt: Arrange the following code lines into the correct order to define a class and create an instance:
items.explanation: The class must be defined before it can be instantiated. The `__init__` method belongs inside the class block, indented under the class header. Only after the class exists can you create an instance with `Book('Python Basics')`.

micro_lesson.title: Accessing Attributes with Dot Notation
micro_lesson.content:
Once an object is created, you access its attributes and methods using dot notation. The object name is followed by a dot and the attribute name. This is the standard pattern for interacting with instances. For example:

```python
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

p = Person('Alice')
print(p.name)
```

The expression `p.name` retrieves the value stored in the `name` attribute of the `p` object.

items.prompt: Complete the statement: `print(p.___)`
items.explanation: Dot notation (`object.attribute`) is used to access attributes of an instance. Here, `p.name` accesses the `name` attribute set in the `__init__` method.

micro_lesson.title: Algorithm: Create Objects and Call Methods
micro_lesson.content:
A common algorithm when working with classes involves creating multiple instances and interacting with them. The steps are: define the class, instantiate objects, modify attributes, and call methods. Here is a complete example:

```python
class Calculator:
    def add(self, a, b):
        return a + b

c1 = Calculator()
c2 = Calculator()
result = c1.add(3, 5)
print(result)
```

First, the class is defined. Then two objects `c1` and `c2` are created. Finally, the `add` method is called on `c1` with arguments `3` and `5`, and the result is printed.

items.prompt: Order the following steps to implement the algorithm of creating two Calculator objects and printing the sum of 4 and 6:
items.explanation: The class must be defined before any instances exist. After instantiation, you can call methods on the objects. The order ensures valid syntax and correct execution flow.

micro_lesson.title: Idiomatic Class Instantiation and Attribute Access
micro_lesson.content:
A common Python idiom is to create a class with a descriptive name, instantiate it with meaningful arguments, and access attributes directly. This pattern makes code readable and maintainable. For example:

```python
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        self.width = width
        self.height = height

r = Rectangle(10, 5)
print(r.width * r.height)
```

Here, `Rectangle` models a geometric shape, `r` is a specific instance, and the area is computed by multiplying the instance attributes.

items.prompt: Fill in the blank to complete the idiom: `r = Rectangle(___, ___)`
items.explanation: The `Rectangle` constructor expects `width` and `height` arguments. Passing `10` and `5` creates a rectangle with those dimensions, which is a standard and readable idiom.

micro_lesson.title: Diagnosing Common OOP Mistakes
micro_lesson.content: When working with objects and classes, beginners often confuse class attributes with instance attributes, or forget to use self correctly. In Python, instance methods must include self as the first parameter to access instance data. Another frequent error is trying to call a method on the class instead of an instance. Always verify that you instantiate a class before accessing instance-specific behavior, and remember that methods defined inside a class automatically receive the instance as self. Below is a buggy example to analyze.

items.prompt: Identify and explain the errors in the following code.
items.hint: Check how methods are defined and called. Consider whether bark can be invoked directly on the class without an instance.
items.explanation: The error occurs at print(Dog.bark()). bark is an instance method requiring self, so it cannot be called directly on the class without providing an instance. The corrected version either removes that line or passes an instance explicitly.

items.prompt: Fix the code so the Rectangle class correctly computes area.
items.hint: In the area method, height is referenced without self. It should be self.height.
items.explanation: The method area tried to access height as a local variable, but it is stored as an instance attribute self.height. Adding self fixes the NameError and returns the correct area.

items.prompt: Fix the edge case where dividing by zero occurs in the Circle class.
items.hint: Returning 0 for a non-positive radius hides invalid input. Consider raising an exception to signal misuse.
items.explanation: The original code silently returned 0 for radius 0, which is misleading. Raising ValueError makes the edge case explicit and prevents incorrect calculations.

micro_lesson.title: Runtime Errors in Object-Oriented Programs
micro_lesson.content: Runtime errors happen when code executes but encounters an invalid operation, such as accessing an attribute that does not exist or calling a method on the wrong object. In OOP, a common runtime issue is AttributeError when an instance lacks the expected attribute due to a typo or missing initialization. Another runtime pitfall is modifying a mutable default argument in a class method, which can cause shared state across instances. Always initialize attributes in __init__ and verify object types before operations.

items.prompt: Explain the runtime error in the following snippet.
items.hint: The method increment is defined but never called before print. Also check whether increment exists on the instance.
items.explanation: The runtime error is actually a logical error: increment is defined but not invoked, so count remains 0. If increment were missing entirely, an AttributeError would occur at c.increment().

items.prompt: Repair the logic in the Student class so average returns the correct mean of marks.
items.hint: The average formula adds an extra 1, which inflates the result. Remove the + 1.
items.explanation: The original code incorrectly added 1 to the mean. The correct average is total divided by the number of marks, yielding 90.0 for the given data.

items.prompt: Given the class hierarchy below, identify what is printed when run and fix the code so that both 'describe' calls produce valid output without errors. A Car class inherits from Vehicle and overrides describe. An instance of Car is created with brand 'Honda'.
items.hint: The original code is valid Python; the challenge is to predict output and demonstrate polymorphic behavior by calling describe on both a Car and a Vehicle instance.

items.prompt: Design a class 'BankAccount' to model a simple bank account. It should store owner_name, balance, and account_number. Include methods to deposit(amount), withdraw(amount) with validation (no negative amounts, no overdraft), and display_balance(). Use encapsulation: keep balance 'private' via name mangling and provide a getter. Create an instance, perform a deposit of 500, a withdrawal of 200, and print the final balance.

test_cases.expected_output:
0
acc.deposit(500)
assert acc.get_balance() == 500
acc.withdraw(200)
assert acc.get_balance() == 300
acc.display_balance()
test_cases.description:
Verifies: acc = BankAccount('Alice', '123456')
assert acc.get_balance() == 0
acc.deposit(500)
assert acc.get_balance() == 500
acc.withdraw(200)
assert acc.get_balance() == 300

Verifies: acc2 = BankAccount('Bob', '654321')
acc2.deposit(-50)
assert acc2.get_balance() == 0

items.hint: Use double underscores for name mangling on balance and validate inputs in deposit and withdraw.
items.explanation: Real-world modeling requires encapsulation to protect internal state and validation to maintain invariants. Name mangling (__balance) discourages direct external mutation, while methods enforce business rules.

items.prompt: Extend BankAccount so that adding two BankAccount instances with '+' creates a new BankAccount whose balance is the sum of both balances, and printing the object shows 'BankAccount(owner=<name>, balance=<amount>)'. Implement __add__ and __str__. Then test with acc1 = BankAccount('Alice', '001', 300) and acc2 = BankAccount('Bob', '002', 400); print(acc1 + acc2).

test_cases.input:
acc1 = BankAccount('Alice', '001', 300)
acc2 = BankAccount('Bob', '002', 400)
result = acc1 + acc2
assert result.get_balance()
test_cases.description:
Verifies: acc1 = BankAccount('Alice', '001', 300)
acc2 = BankAccount('Bob', '002', 400)
result = acc1 + acc2
assert result.get_balance() == 700
assert str(result) == 'BankAccount(owner=Alice & Bob, balance=700)'

items.hint: In __add__, check isinstance(other, BankAccount), access __balance via name mangling, and return a new instance. In __str__, construct the string representation manually.
items.explanation: Operator overloading via magic methods like __add__ and __str__ enables intuitive syntax and clean output. Mastery here means combining encapsulation, validation, inheritance awareness, and protocol-based design into a cohesive, reusable class.
